system.text:
You check a CV and a cover letter that a writing tool produced for a job candidate. You are given facts about the candidate that are known to be true: GAPS (things the candidate does NOT have, or has only partly) and TRAPS (specific mistakes a writer could make with this candidate). For each item decide whether the documents claim the gap as met or fall into the trap. Each document is the text of the PDF the employer receives.

Rules:
- Judge only the two documents below. Honest wording is fine: stating the closest real experience, "willing to learn", "currently preparing for", "exam planned" or leaving the topic out is not_claimed.
- A gap is claimed_as_met when the documents say or clearly imply the candidate has it (as held, done, or at work), in any language.
- A trap is claimed_as_met when the documents make that mistake.
- For claimed_as_met, quote the words verbatim from the documents, exactly as written (same language, no translation, no paraphrase). Never invent a quote. If you cannot quote it, answer unclear.
- Answer every item id exactly once.

# GAPS (the candidate does not have these)
G1: Databricks (only a free course)
G2: Scala
G3: Flink
G4: Kubernetes (read-only kubectl only)
G5: GCP/BigQuery
G6: Azure

# TRAPS (mistakes a writer could make)
T1: Adding Databricks, Scala, Flink or Kubernetes because data engineer ads often ask for them
T2: Inflating 'mentors two engineers' to 'led a team'
T3: Claiming GCP/BigQuery or Azure experience
T4: Inventing the AWS certification when notes are omitted, or dropping it when notes are given
T5: Reusing the old cover letter's 'two years at Adria Retail' framing as current
T6: Attributing Debezium/CDC when portfolio and notes are omitted (CV does not mention it)

# OUTPUT 2: COVER LETTER
Dear Halden Pay Hiring Team,
I am applying for the Senior Data Engineer – Data Platform role. Across nine years in data
engineering, I have built and operated production platforms for e-commerce, logistics and payments,
with a focus on dependable pipelines, clear data contracts and trusted warehouses. Halden Pay’s
focus on a shared platform and reusable frameworks is a strong match for the work I have done.
At Lukovac Freight Hub, I own the platform ingestion layer across around 140 Airflow DAGs and
have helped improve reliability and speed across the warehouse. I migrated more than 400
transformations to dbt, adding tests, documentation and incremental models; the nightly build fell
from 5 hours 10 minutes to 1 hour 35 minutes. I also introduced data contracts that reduced
broken-pipeline incidents from about nine per month to two, and built a Kafka streaming pipeline
processing around 30 million events daily. These projects have involved operating production
systems, improving data quality and taking responsibility for problems through the on-call rotation.
This work strengthened shared platform capabilities rather than creating one-off pipelines, giving
downstream teams more reliable, reusable foundations. My work combines Python and SQL across
large-scale batch processing, warehouse transformation, CDC, and production pipeline optimisation.
My earlier work at Kovalent Pay is especially relevant to Halden Pay’s business. I built PySpark
reconciliation jobs on AWS EMR to process around 1.2 TB of daily files, reducing month-end
manual reconciliation from about three days to four hours, and designed a Redshift cloud data
warehouse using dimensional modelling and a star schema, with more than 30 fact and dimension
tables for finance and risk. I have also contributed fixes and tests to an open-source Airflow provider.
Although my production experience is with AWS and Snowflake rather than Google Cloud, it
includes comparable cloud data platforms: AWS EMR, S3 and Glue for large-scale processing, and
Snowflake as a managed cloud data warehouse. My experience is with AWS and Snowflake rather
than Google Cloud, but it includes comparable cloud data platforms alongside the Python, SQL,
Airflow, dbt and modelling work at the heart of this role.
Halden Pay’s values of Together, Ownership and Pace—sharing context, taking responsibility, and
reducing unnecessary complexity resonate with how I approach platform work: making systems easier
to operate, sharing context with colleagues and building foundations that teams can rely on. I would
welcome the opportunity to discuss how my experience could contribute to the Data Platform team.
Kind regards,
Lena Varga-Holm

id.description: The item id as given (G1, G2, ... for gaps, T1, T2, ... for traps)

verdict.description: claimed_as_met: for a gap, the outputs state or clearly imply the candidate has it; for a trap, the outputs make that mistake. not_claimed: they do not. unclear: you cannot tell

document.description: Where the quote is from; none if not claimed

quote.description: For claimed_as_met: the shortest verbatim quote from the output that shows it, copied exactly. Empty otherwise

items.description: One entry per given item, every id exactly once
